public_rationale: The claim is that LLMs fell short of human-level reliability and generalization at the time of the post. The evidence from late 2024 backs this. ARC Prize's analysis of o3, the strongest system then, said it was not AGI and still failed some very easy tasks. Early ARC-AGI-2 tests put it under 30% where smart humans scored over 95%. Apple researchers found that every model tested lost accuracy when only the numbers in grade-school math problems changed. There is real counterevidence: o3's 75.7% on ARC-AGI-1 was called a genuine breakthrough in adapting to novel tasks. But Marcus said 'reliably' generalize. The same source still judged o3 far from human-level, so the core claim holds.
limitations: The o3 result shows the gap was narrowing fast.
The perturbation study covers math word problems only.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: LLMs do not meet his AGI definition: they are unreliable and cannot reliably generalize to novel circumstances.

statement.excerpt: LLMs don’t meet that; as the world has discovered, reliability is not their strong suit; as I have often written here, and as Goertzel also emphasizes, LLMs lack the ability to reliably generalize to novel circumstances.

from_speaker: flexible and general, with resourcefulness and reliability comparable to (or beyond) human intelligence
reliability is not their strong suit
LLMs lack the ability to reliably generalize to novel circumstances
our_interpretation: Plain reading: as of the post, the best LLMs did not reach human-level reliability and generalization. In particular, their performance on new or slightly changed tasks was not dependable.
He named no period. I use the latest evaluations public before the post, October 2024 to the post date (2025-01-13), covering the o1/o3, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 generation.
'Reliably' matters. Some success on new tasks does not contradict the claim. Robust, human-comparable generalization would.
criteria.support_condition: Evaluations from the period show frontier LLMs failing tasks that are easy for humans on novel benchmarks, or losing much accuracy when problems are lightly changed. Expert evaluators judge them short of human-level general intelligence.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evaluations from the period show frontier LLMs matching humans on novel, out-of-distribution tasks and holding steady under such changes.

evidence.explanation: The benchmark's creator says that even the strongest system of the time still failed very easy novel tasks and was not human-level general intelligence.

evidence.explanation: Early tests showed a large gap between the best model and humans on fresh novel tasks. That fits a lack of reliable generalization.

evidence.excerpt: Specifically, the performance of all models declines when only the numerical values in the question are altered in the GSM-Symbolic benchmark.
evidence.explanation: Every model tested got worse when only the numbers in familiar problems changed. That shows unreliable generalization to slightly new cases. The page read is v2; v1 was posted 2024-10-07.

evidence.excerpt: OpenAI's new o3 model represents a significant leap forward in AI's ability to adapt to novel tasks.
evidence.locator: section 'OpenAI o3 ARC-AGI Results', paragraph after results table
evidence.explanation: o3 showed a real jump in adapting to novel tasks (75.7% on ARC-AGI-1). That partly cuts against a flat 'lack the ability to generalize', though not against 'reliably' or human-level.
